title: RBAC: who can do what
summary: Roles, bindings and service accounts, and how to check permissions.

steps.title: Four objects
body: Role         (namespaced)  rules: verbs on resources in ONE namespace
ClusterRole  (cluster)     same rules, usable in every namespace or for cluster-wide things (nodes)
RoleBinding                gives a Role or ClusterRole to subjects, inside ONE namespace
ClusterRoleBinding         gives a ClusterRole to subjects everywhere
roleRef: { kind: Role, name: pod-reader, apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io }
RBAC is **allow-only**: no deny rules. Anything not granted is forbidden (`Error from server (Forbidden)`).
Subjects are Users and Groups (from your identity provider, e.g. Entra ID) and **ServiceAccounts** (identities for pods: `system:serviceaccount:shop:shop-api`).

steps.prompt: A RoleBinding in namespace `shop` refers to the ClusterRole `view`. What does the subject get?
options: Read access to most resources, but only in `shop`
steps.explain: This is the usual pattern: define a role once as a ClusterRole (`view`, `edit`, `admin` are built in) and bind it per namespace.

steps.prompt: Let the `ci-deployer` service account in `shop` update Deployments there.
code: roleRef: { kind: Role, name: deployer, apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io }
steps.explain: Deployments live in the `apps` group (the core group is written as an empty string `""`, never `core`). `kubectl apply` needs `patch` (and `create` for new objects).

steps.title: Check before you guess
body: kubectl auth can-i list secrets -n shop
kubectl auth can-i create deployments -n shop --as=system:serviceaccount:shop:ci-deployer
- Give each workload its own ServiceAccount; set `automountServiceAccountToken: false` for pods that never call the API.
- Avoid `cluster-admin` bindings for people and CI; prefer namespace-scoped `edit`.
- `list`/`watch` on Secrets reveals every value, and `create pods` in a namespace lets someone mount any Secret there. Treat both as sensitive.
- Wildcards (`"*"`) in verbs or resources grow silently as new resources appear.

steps.prompt: A RoleBinding in namespace `shop` grants Role `pod-reader` (get/list/watch on pods and pods/log in core group) to user `ana`. What can ana do?
steps.explain: `pods/log` is a subresource and must be granted explicitly; Deployments are in the `apps` group, which the role does not cover.

steps.prompt: CI fails with `deployments.apps "shop-api" is forbidden: User "system:serviceaccount:ci:runner" cannot patch resource "deployments" in API group "apps" in the namespace "shop"`. Which fix follows least privilege?
options: A Role in `shop` allowing get/patch/update on deployments in `apps`, bound to that service account
Give the service account `edit` across all namespaces with a ClusterRoleBinding
Run CI with your personal kubeconfig
steps.explain: The error message tells you exactly what is missing: verb, resource, API group, namespace and subject.

steps.prompt: Fill in what this command prints when the service account has no permission to delete pods.
code: $ kubectl auth can-i delete pods -n shop --as=system:serviceaccount:shop:shop-api
steps.explain: `can-i` prints `yes` or `no` (and exits 0 or 1), which makes it handy in scripts and CI checks.

steps.title: Give CI exactly the access it needs
prompt: This terminal runs a **real one-node Kubernetes 1.37 cluster** (k3s) with `kubectl` (alias `k`). The CI pipeline will deploy to the namespace `shop` with its own identity. Create:
2. a Role `deployer` in `shop` that can `get`, `list`, `watch`, `patch` and `update` Deployments, and `get` and
`list` pods (to watch a rollout), and nothing else;
3. a RoleBinding that gives the Role to the ServiceAccount.

checks.name: ci-deployer can update Deployments in shop
checks.cmd: kubectl auth can-i patch deployments -n shop --as=system:serviceaccount:shop:ci-deployer; kubectl auth can-i get deployments -n shop --as=system:serviceaccount:shop:ci-deployer; kubectl auth can-i list pods -n shop --as=system:serviceaccount:shop:ci-deployer
checks.fail: The service account `ci-deployer` in `shop` should be able to `get`/`list`/`watch`/`patch`/`update` Deployments and `get`/`list` pods there.

checks.name: and nothing more
checks.cmd: for q in 'delete deployments -n shop' 'get secrets -n shop' 'patch deployments -n payments' 'create clusterrolebindings'; do kubectl auth can-i $q --as=system:serviceaccount:shop:ci-deployer; done
checks.fail: `ci-deployer` may do more than it should (delete, read Secrets, other namespaces or cluster-wide). Use a namespaced Role with only those verbs.

checks.name: it is a Role and a RoleBinding in shop
checks.cmd: kubectl -n shop get rolebinding -o json | jq -r '.items[] | select(.subjects[]? | .kind=="ServiceAccount" and .name=="ci-deployer") | .roleRef.kind' | sort -u
checks.fail: Bind it with a RoleBinding in `shop` to a Role (not a ClusterRole binding).

hints: `kubectl -n shop create role deployer --verb=get,list,watch,patch,update --resource=deployments`, then add the pods rule (`kubectl -n shop patch role deployer --type=json ...`, or write the YAML with two rules).
`kubectl -n shop create rolebinding ci-deployer --role=deployer --serviceaccount=shop:ci-deployer`, then `kubectl auth can-i --list -n shop --as=system:serviceaccount:shop:ci-deployer`.
solution: kubectl auth can-i patch deployments -n shop --as=system:serviceaccount:shop:ci-deployer
kubectl auth can-i get secrets -n shop --as=system:serviceaccount:shop:ci-deployer
steps.explain: RBAC is allow-only: a subject can do exactly what its bindings grant and nothing else, and a RoleBinding scopes even a ClusterRole to one namespace. `kubectl auth can-i --as` checks it without logging in as anyone. Note what is missing on purpose: `delete`, and Secrets (whoever can read Secrets in a namespace effectively has every credential in it).
